commits.message:
test(strip): pin edge styles resolving against the render's theme (rich-style-tdn)

Every cell in this suite carried a literal style definition and OPTIONS
never carried a Theme, so nothing exercised the behaviour this branch
introduced: an edge style that is a theme name is a colour only against
the theme of the render drawing it.

That left the deferral unpinned. A joiner that read edgeStyle eagerly in
join(), instead of inside the renderable it returns, passed every case in
the file — there was no theme for it to lose. The joiner case fails under
exactly that mutation; both cases fail when resolvedStyle drops
options.theme.

fix(panel): resolve a RichText accessory's style as the text itself does (rich-style-tdn)

Text forgives a style name the render's theme does not define: it draws
with no style. Panel resolved a RichText accessory's style with the
strict getStyle instead, so an accessory whose style no theme defines
threw inside a panel while the same text rendered itself without
complaint. Before this branch it drew in the border style.

RichText.resolvedStyle(options) is the text's own style resolved through
the one forgiving rule text.ts already holds. Panel's accessory calls
it, and so do RichText's edgeStyle and render, which made the same call
inline.

Tests:
- panel: an accessory whose style name no theme defines renders the
  same segments as an accessory with no style.
- console: a console style and a print style that only the console's
  theme defines each draw in the theme's colour.

fix(template-bindings): keep the parser's reason when a fragment's base style does not parse (rich-style-tdn)

A scope fragment whose base style fails Style.parse threw a TypeError
calling the string "the name", but a StyleSyntaxError proves only that
the string is not a definition: "not" and "on" are malformed
definitions, not theme names. Only the theme of a render can tell a name
from a typo, so the template layer does not guess. The message now says
the base style is not a style definition, and the StyleSyntaxError rides
along as the cause.

Tests: a name ("repr.number") and a malformed definition ("not") each
throw a TypeError whose cause is the StyleSyntaxError.

fix(tree,text): keep theme resolution out of Tree.measure and the highlightWords count (rich-style-tdn)

Tree.measure walks the same rows render does, and that walk resolved
each row's guide style through getStyle. A guide_style name the theme
did not define made measure throw, though a width needs no style. Rows
now carry their guide styles as given, nearest first, and _renderRow
resolves them and draws the guides in the first that is not null.
Python Rich's Tree.__rich_measure__ resolves no style either.

highlightWords returned 0 for an empty style, while _addSpan already
drops one. That return is gone, so the count is the words matched for
any style, as in Python Rich's highlight_words. Checking a name there
instead would bring back the theme-blind lookup this branch removes.

Tests:
- tree: a guide style name no theme defines measures as no guide style
  does.
- text: highlightWords counts every match for an undefined name and for
  the empty style.
- console: a word highlighted with a name only the console's theme
  defines is counted and drawn in the theme's colour.

fix(template-bindings): style a scope fragment whose base style is a definition (rich-style-tdn)

applyStyleToFragment rejected every string base style, so a RichText
handed in through template scope with the style "italic" could not be
made bold. It now parses a string base as a style definition and throws
its TypeError only when that parse fails, which is what a theme name
does: a name resolves against the theme of a render, and a template runs
before any render exists.

The link-sanitizer comment in RichText no longer promises that a raw
richText.style.link is clean. It names the two crossings instead:
admitStyle on the way in, resolveStyle on the way out to a render.

Tests:
- test/core/base-style.ts holds baseStyleOf, the one narrowing of
  RichText.style to a Style. The style-funcs, color-funcs and text tests
  read style attributes through it, because String.prototype's legacy
  bold and link methods let a raw rt.style.bold type-check and compare
  a function to true.
- style-funcs: {{ bold .n }} over a scope RichText styled italic comes
  out bold and italic.
- console: a Table under Theme({}, { inherit: false }) throws
  StyleSyntaxError. Thirteen renderables (Panel border and title, Rule,
  Tree guide, Padding, Spinner, ProgressBar, the percentage, remaining
  and elapsed progress columns, Markdown heading and inline code,
  Traceback) and Status each draw two theme colours as truecolor SGR.

fix(style)!: resolve style names against the console theme (rich-style-tdn)

`new Console({ theme })` changed nothing. Every style name was resolved when
its renderable or span was built, through the built-in defaults inside
`Style.parse`, before any console could offer a theme, and `Console` stored the
theme it was given without ever reading it. Names now resolve when they
render, in the theme of the console doing the printing, as they do in Rich.

- `Theme.resolve(style)` is the one lookup from a name to a style. It stays
  outside `Style.parse`'s process-wide cache, so two consoles with different
  themes cannot bleed into each other. `Style.parse` parses definitions only.
- `RenderOptions.theme` carries the printing console's theme, and every
  renderable resolves its style names in `render` through one internal
  resolver in `protocol.ts`. Table cells and titles now spread the render
  options instead of building a fresh literal, so the theme reaches them.
- `RichText` keeps its base and span styles as given and resolves them at
  render.
- Template style functions throw a `TypeError` for a fragment whose base style
  is a name: a template runs before any render exists, so the name has no
  theme to resolve against.

Breaking:
- `StyledRenderable.edgeStyle(side)` is now `edgeStyle(side, options)`, and a
  joiner reads edges inside the `render` of the renderable it returns. The
  built-in joiners do.
- `Style.parse` no longer accepts a name: `Style.parse("repr.number")` throws
  `StyleSyntaxError`. Use `Theme.resolve`.
- `RichText.style` is `string | Style`.
- A renderable resolves its style strings at render, so a name its theme lacks
  throws `StyleSyntaxError` when it is printed. Under
  `new Theme(..., { inherit: false })` that includes built-in names such as
  `table.header`, which used to resolve whatever the theme.

docs/style.md, highlighting.md, strip.md and protocol.md describe the new
behaviour, and every changed snippet was compiled and run in a consumer
project.

docs(highlighting): make the custom highlighter examples run (rich-docs-lxn, rich-docs-vaa) (#118)

RequestHighlighter could not run as written. Its patterns used Python's
(?P<name>) group syntax, which a JavaScript RegExp literal rejects. It
set highlights and baseStyle as instance fields, but RegexHighlighter
reads them from the class, so it would have highlighted nothing. It
called the highlighter as a function instead of through .call(). Its
per-group styles also relied on a Console looking http.method up in the
Theme it was given, and no Console does that (rich-style-tdn). The
example now uses static fields and one literal baseStyle, and the page
says which names a baseStyle ending in "." can produce.

RainbowHighlighter passed stylize its arguments as (start, end, style),
but the signature is (style, start, end). It also used Console without
importing it.

The opening example said ReprHighlighter styles file paths, True and a
UUID. It has no path pattern and matches only lowercase true and false,
and the example's "a3f2-..." was styled as a quoted string. The example
and both pattern lists now name only what it styles (rich-docs-vaa).

Both custom highlighter blocks, copied from the page into a TypeScript
project that depends on the package, type-check under strict and
noUncheckedIndexedAccess and print the styles the page describes.
